title: Park County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Park County wells have a median depth of 240 ft and yield of 5.5 gpm. Review local drilling costs, bedrock risks and what to check before buying.
h1: Planning for a Well in Park County
intro_html:
A well near Bailey can behave differently from one outside Hartsel or Fairplay. In Park County's fractured mountain ground, the useful question is not just how deep neighboring wells went, but what water they found and whether it held up under pumping.

Colorado DWR records include 22,661 permitted wells in Park County, with 15,366 recorded as constructed. Reported wells have a median depth of 240 feet and a median pump yield of 5.5 gpm. Those are useful starting points for a property search—not promises for an individual lot.

sections.heading: A 240-Foot Starting Point, Not a Bailey-to-Hartsel Rule
sections.html:
Among the 16,108 wells reporting depth, Park County's median is 240 feet. The middle half runs from 140 to 380 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 520 feet. For a drilling bid, that spread matters more than the median alone: ask what additional footage costs and how the contractor handles a hole that must go deeper than expected.

The permit aquifer field is dominated by unnamed or fractured-bedrock entries, with fractured crystalline and granite also identified. Water moves through fractures rather than a uniformly productive layer. A nearby successful well is useful evidence, but it cannot establish where your lot will intercept water. Compare records around the actual parcel in Bailey, Como or Guffey before using a countywide depth for budgeting.

sections.heading: What Park County's 5.5 GPM Median Means at the House
sections.html:
The 9,476 wells with reported pump yields have a median of 5.5 gpm, with the middle half between 3.0 and 9.0 gpm. A reported yield in that range can support household use with appropriate pumping and storage, but the number alone does not tell you how the well handles sustained demand.

Reported yields fall below 1 gpm for 5% of wells. That is a meaningful buying risk: a low-producing well may need storage and careful demand management, and it deserves closer testing before closing. Another 57% report 5–15 gpm. Ask for the pumping-test duration, drawdown and recovery information rather than treating the permit's yield entry as a current performance guarantee.

sections.heading: Water Levels Are Deeper in Recent Park County Records
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the bottom of the hole. Among 1,700 reporting wells, the median is 100 feet below ground, with the middle half between 55 and 160 feet. Pump placement and pumping drawdown still need separate evaluation.

The decade medians show deeper water in later records: 40 feet in the 1960s, 58 in the 1970s, and 60 in the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s. The median reaches 103 feet in the 2010s and is 100 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels over the longer record, but it does not prove a countywide falling water table. These are different groups of wells, not repeated measurements of the same wells.

sections.heading: Park County's Permit History and Recorded Drillers
sections.html:
The largest permit decade was the 1990s, with 5,691 permits, followed by 4,331 in the 2000s. Records show 2,018 in the 2010s and 1,641 in the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. The current decade is incomplete, so its total is not directly comparable with a full decade. Permit issuance also is not the same as completed construction.

The most active drillers in the records are Allen Drilling & Excavating Co., Inc. (Allen, Jack R.), with 3,726; Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert), with 1,482; and Stan'S Drilling (Stansbury, Larry), with 952. Those historical counts can help you recognize names on neighboring well reports, but they do not establish current availability.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well in Park County Bedrock
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $65–$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock such as granite and gneiss. At the 240-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $15,600–$24,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $21,600–$36,000.

Treat those figures as planning allowances, not a parcel-specific quote. The 140–380-foot middle depth range leaves substantial room for the final footage to change. Get a written scope that explains casing, grout, testing, drilling access and the route from the well to the house. On a mountain lot, access preparation and utility routing deserve attention before a drilling rig is scheduled. Confirm which site-work items are included and which are separate.

sections.heading: Mine Features, Water Testing and Low-Yield Ground
sections.html:
The mapped environmental inventory within about 10 miles includes 3 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 31 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. Those entries are reasons to investigate the parcel's surroundings; they do not establish that a particular household well is contaminated. Sampling locations and cleanup sites need to be evaluated in relation to the property.

Before buying, arrange laboratory water testing and discuss locally appropriate testing with the county or a qualified water professional. Inspect the wellhead, casing and available grout records. Fractured rock can produce low yields or an unsuccessful hole even near a working well. For a build, coordinate the well location with septic siting, required separations, drainage and building access before committing to the site layout.

sections.heading: Before Closing on Land in Fairplay, Jefferson or Lake George
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit and the closest useful well records, not just the listing description. Domestic/household use appears on 91% of Park County permits, but that does not mean every permit allows outdoor watering, livestock or every proposed use. Read the actual authorization and confirm that it fits your plans.

For an existing home, obtain the well construction report, pump information, water-quality results and a current performance evaluation. For vacant land around Fairplay, Jefferson or Lake George, verify permit eligibility before treating water as settled. Exempt household-use permits can carry tight use restrictions, and some proposals in over-appropriated basins may require augmentation. Settle those questions alongside drilling access, septic feasibility and the house location—not after buying the lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Park County, Colorado?
faq.a: Park County wells have a median reported depth of 240 feet. The middle half runs from 140 to 380 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 520 feet. Fractured bedrock makes individual results variable, so use nearby construction records and a footage-based drilling quote rather than assuming your lot will match the median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Park County?
faq.a: The Park County cost model uses $65–$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the median depth of 240 feet, the drilled hole is about $15,600–$24,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $21,600–$36,000. Confirm casing, grout, access work and other scope details in the written bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Park County?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 5.5 gpm, and the middle half is 3.0–9.0 gpm. Reported yields are below 1 gpm for 5% of wells. Before buying, have the existing well's sustained output, drawdown and recovery evaluated. A historical yield entry does not guarantee present performance or establish how much storage the household needs.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Park County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established by testing the individual well. The mapped inventory within about 10 miles includes 3 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 31 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites, but proximity alone does not prove contamination. Review nearby site information, inspect the well's condition and arrange laboratory testing appropriate to the property.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Park County?
faq.a: The recorded decade medians suggest deeper water over the longer term: 40 feet below ground in the 1960s, 60 in the 2000s, 103 in the 2010s and 100 in the 2020s. These are different groups of wells, so they do not prove a countywide decline. Evaluate the property's own water-level and pumping history where available.
